findings.explanation: HLD_CI_017 (unpinned reusable-workflow call, HIGH/supply-chain) is correctly detected and then suppressed with '# holden:ignore:HLD_CI_017: its by design' — a reason that doesn't address the actual risk. This job runs on every push to main with permissions: {contents: write, id-token: write} and calls JamesWoolfenden/.github/.github/workflows/terraform-verify-gcp.yml@main, an unpinned mutable ref. If that ref is ever compromised (repo takeover, force-push, or a GitHub ref-resolution race), the attacker's workflow code executes with a GCP OIDC token for terraform-gcp-cloudrun@pike-477416.iam.gserviceaccount.com and write access to this repo, automatically, with no PR review gate. 'It's my project' doesn't mitigate a supply-chain compromise of a *different* repo (JamesWoolfenden/.github) that this workflow trusts implicitly. pull_request.yml:16-18 has the identical pattern (gated behind a PR at least, so lower blast radius, but same weak justification). Re-checked 2026-11-20: the reusable workflow is still referenced at @main; the suppression reason now reads 'its by design', which still doesn't address the risk.
findings.fix:
Replace lines 18-20 of .github/workflows/verify.yml:
  verify:
    uses: JamesWoolfenden/.github/.github/workflows/terraform-verify-gcp.yml@7e6376f276d0f76e4565243d9c443330804b960e
    with:
      service_account: terraform-gcp-cloudrun@pike-477416.iam.gserviceaccount.com
(dropping the '# holden:ignore:HLD_CI_017' comment on the line above, since it's no longer needed once pinned)
findings.remediation: Pin both reusable-workflow refs to the current commit SHA of JamesWoolfenden/.github's main branch (verified via `gh api repos/JamesWoolfenden/.github/git/refs/heads/main`): 7e6376f276d0f76e4565243d9c443330804b960e. Both target files exist at that SHA (terraform-verify-gcp.yml, terraform-pr-gcp.yml). Drop the now-unneeded ignore comment once pinned, and consider Renovate/Dependabot for periodic SHA bumps so pinning doesn't silently freeze out fixes from the upstream reusable workflow.
findings.title: HLD_CI_017 suppressed with a non-substantive reason on a push-to-main workflow with contents:write + id-token:write

findings.explanation: Same HLD_CI_017 suppression pattern as HOLDEN_AI_001, on the PR-triggered job. Lower blast radius than verify.yml since it's gated behind a pull_request event rather than a direct push to main, but it still mints a GCP OIDC token (id-token: write) against an unpinned @main ref during CI on every PR, including from forks if the workflow trigger ever changes to pull_request_target or a fork-based contributor model is adopted later. Re-checked 2026-11-20: the reusable workflow is still referenced at @main; the suppression reason now reads 'its by design', which still doesn't address the risk.
findings.fix:
Replace lines 16-20 of .github/workflows/pull_request.yml:
  pr:
    uses: JamesWoolfenden/.github/.github/workflows/terraform-pr-gcp.yml@7e6376f276d0f76e4565243d9c443330804b960e
    with:
      service_account: terraform-gcp-cloudrun@pike-477416.iam.gserviceaccount.com
(dropping the '# holden:ignore:HLD_CI_017' comment on the line above)
findings.remediation: Pin to the same commit SHA as HOLDEN_AI_001: 7e6376f276d0f76e4565243d9c443330804b960e (terraform-pr-gcp.yml confirmed present at that SHA).
findings.title: Same unpinned-reusable-workflow pattern as verify.yml, weaker blast radius but same non-substantive suppression

findings.explanation: This module always creates a google_monitoring_uptime_check_config targeting the service's public .run.app URI via the default global (public) checker locations — it never sets checker_type/internal_checkers for a VPC-based private check. But var.service.ingress lets callers restrict the service to INGRESS_TRAFFIC_INTERNAL_ONLY or INGRESS_TRAFFIC_INTERNAL_LOAD_BALANCER, and Google's public uptime checkers run outside the customer's VPC — Cloud Run's ingress control blocks them just like any other external caller. All three real instantiations in this repo's own examples use a restricted ingress value, so their uptime checks will permanently fail, not because the service is unhealthy but because the monitoring config itself can never reach it. HLD_GCP_336 only verifies an uptime check exists, so it can't see that the check is structurally unreachable for its own target. Net effect: a false 'service down' signal (or a check silently ignored by whoever's on call once it's learned to always be red), which is worse than no check for a reliability/on-call workflow.
findings.remediation: Either (a) skip creating the uptime check when var.service.ingress != "INGRESS_TRAFFIC_ALL" (count/for_each guard), or (b) switch to a VPC-based private uptime check (checker_type = "VPC_CHECKERS" with internal_checkers referencing a checker deployed inside the same VPC as the vpc_connector) when ingress is restricted. Which is correct depends on whether restricted-ingress deployments are expected to have monitoring at all — that's a product decision for this module's maintainer, not something to guess.
findings.title: Uptime check monitors the public URI even when the service's own ingress setting blocks public traffic

findings.explanation: google_cloud_run_v2_service.tf:151-157 already creates a google_kms_crypto_key_iam_member granting roles/cloudkms.cryptoKeyEncrypterDecrypter to the Cloud Run service agent whenever var.encryption_key != null — this fires once per module instantiation. Both examples then also declare an identical, hand-written google_kms_crypto_key_iam_member for the exact same role/member/key at the call site. examplea ends up with 2 Terraform resources managing 1 real IAM binding; examplemulti (which calls the module twice, as frontend and backend) ends up with 3. This isn't wrong at the GCP API level (IAM member bindings are idempotent/additive), but it's dead weight that muddies which resource is actually load-bearing, and it sets a confusing precedent for anyone copying these examples as a template — they'd reasonably assume the caller is responsible for granting KMS access, when the module already does it.
related_resources: google_cloud_run_v2_service.tf:151 (google_kms_crypto_key_iam_member.cloud_run_service_agent, the module-internal grant this duplicates)
example/examplemulti/module.multi.tf:37 (google_kms_crypto_key_iam_member.cloudrun_sa, same pattern, duplicated twice more via module.frontend + module.backend)
findings.remediation: Decide, deliberately, which layer owns this grant: either the module should be the single source of truth (drop the explicit example-level resources), or the module's internal auto-grant should be removed in favor of requiring callers to grant KMS access themselves (a common pattern where the module doesn't reach out and mutate IAM on externally-owned resources like a caller-created KMS key). Leaving both is not itself dangerous, just redundant — worth a deliberate choice rather than leaving it as accretion.
findings.title: Both examples explicitly grant the KMS decrypt IAM binding that the module already grants internally per-instantiation

findings.explanation: var.worker_pool_service_account and var.legacy_service_account default to "" and their validations accept "", so setting only worker_pool_image or legacy_service_image deploys a workload with no service account, which Cloud Run resolves to PROJECT_NUMBER-compute@developer.gserviceaccount.com (usually project Editor). The main service requires var.service_account, so this is the outlier. HLD_GCP_084 can't see it: the resources are count = 0 in every example, and an empty string passes its not_null check on the v1 resource at evaluation time anyway.
findings.remediation: Reject an empty service account whenever the matching image is set (cross-variable validation), and reject the compute default SA email.
findings.title: Worker pool and legacy v1 service run as the Compute Engine default service account unless the caller remembers to set one

findings.explanation: google_cloud_run_v2_service.default always sets binary_authorization { use_default = true } and passes var.encryption_key, but the worker pool and the v1 service the same module creates set neither. A caller who enabled CMEK and relies on Binary Authorization gets two workloads that bypass both. HLD_GCP_361 (worker pool CMEK) never evaluates because the pool is count = 0 in the examples, and nothing covers worker pool Binary Authorization.
findings.remediation: Add binary_authorization { use_default = true } and encryption_key = var.encryption_key to the worker pool; add the run.googleapis.com/binary-authorization and run.googleapis.com/encryption-key annotations to the v1 template.
findings.title: Worker pool and legacy v1 service skip the Binary Authorization and CMEK controls the module enforces on the main service

findings.explanation: The v1 resource sets no run.googleapis.com/ingress annotation, so it takes Cloud Run's default of "all". A caller who set service.ingress to INGRESS_TRAFFIC_INTERNAL_ONLY and enables legacy_service_image during a migration gets a second, public endpoint for the same workload. IAM still applies (allUsers is rejected), so this is exposure rather than unauthenticated access.
findings.remediation: Map var.service.ingress onto the v1 ingress annotation (all / internal / internal-and-cloud-load-balancing).
findings.title: Legacy v1 service ignores var.service.ingress and is internet-reachable even when the v2 service is internal-only

findings.explanation: data.google_project.current has no project_id, so it resolves the provider default project. When var.project differs, the KMS grant goes to another project's serverless-robot-prod agent (giving an unrelated principal encrypt/decrypt on the key) while the agent that actually runs the service has no access, so revisions fail to start. The worker pool and v1 service also omit project and deploy into the provider project, not the main service's.
findings.remediation: Set project_id = var.project on the data source and project = var.project on the worker pool and v1 service.
findings.title: CMEK service-agent grant and the optional workloads use the provider's default project, not var.project

findings.explanation: worker_pool_image and legacy_service_image reject :latest, but the images for the main service, the one that always deploys, are not checked. HLD_GCP_200 lands on Unknown because the image comes from the variable; the examples pin nginx:1.27.4, so nothing fails today, but a consumer can pass a mutable tag unchecked.
findings.remediation: Add a validation that every containers[].image has a tag other than latest, or a digest.
findings.title: containers[].image has no :latest/untagged validation, unlike the worker pool and legacy images

findings.explanation: var.invokers rejects allUsers, so every service this module creates requires an authenticated caller, yet the public uptime check sends a plain GET to / with no credentials. Cloud Run answers 403 and the check never passes. That means a permanently red alert source rather than monitoring. The principle is a best fit: the issue is broken monitoring, not missing logging.
findings.remediation: Add service_agent_authentication { type = "OIDC_TOKEN" } to the public http_check and have the caller grant roles/run.invoker to the Cloud Monitoring service agent.
findings.title: Public uptime check is unauthenticated against a service the module forces to require IAM, so it can only fail

findings.explanation: The resource reads try(var.service.timeout, "300s") and try(c["resources"], {}), but neither the service nor the containers object type declares timeout or resources. Terraform drops undeclared attributes, so every service runs with a 300s timeout and 1 CPU / 512Mi whatever the caller passes. Workloads that need more memory get OOM-killed with no way to tune it.
findings.remediation: Add timeout = optional(string, "300s") to var.service and resources = optional(object({ limits = optional(map(string)) })) to var.containers.
findings.title: Request timeout and container resource limits are hard-coded because the variable types drop those attributes

findings.explanation: Marking the key name sensitive hides CMEK key changes as (sensitive value) in plans, so a reviewer can't see which key a service is switching to. The value is a resource path, not key material.
findings.fix: Remove the line `sensitive   = true` from variable "encryption_key".
findings.title: encryption_key is marked sensitive although a KMS key resource name is not secret

suggested_policies.rationale: A Cloud Run v2 worker pool with no (or empty) template.service_account runs as the Compute Engine default SA. HLD_GCP_084 covers services but not worker pools; only HLD_GCP_361 (CMEK) covers this type.
suggested_policies.yaml:
id: LOCAL_GCP_001
name: Cloud Run v2 worker pools must run as a dedicated service account
principle: identity-and-access
severity: HIGH
rationale: |
  A worker pool without template.service_account runs as the Compute Engine
  default service account, which usually holds project Editor.
message: |
  google_cloud_run_v2_worker_pool has no dedicated template.service_account.
remediation: |
  Set template.service_account to a least-privilege service account email.
resources:
  google_cloud_run_v2_worker_pool:
    all:
      - path: template.service_account
        not_empty: true
      - path: template.service_account
        not_matches: '-compute@developer\.gserviceaccount\.com$'

suggested_policies.rationale: HLD_GCP_167 requires binary_authorization on Cloud Run v2 services; worker pools accept the same block but nothing checks it, so a pool can deploy unverified images.
suggested_policies.yaml:
id: LOCAL_GCP_002
name: Cloud Run v2 worker pools must enforce Binary Authorization
principle: supply-chain
severity: MEDIUM
rationale: |
  Without a binary_authorization block, images deployed to the worker pool are
  not checked against the Binary Authorization policy.
message: |
  google_cloud_run_v2_worker_pool has no binary_authorization block.
remediation: |
  Add binary_authorization { use_default = true }.
resources:
  google_cloud_run_v2_worker_pool:
    path: binary_authorization
    not_null: true
